name: Olive oil baths

lead: An olive oil bath means adding a small amount of extra virgin olive oil to warm bath water so it coats the skin, leaving it soft and moisturised. The ritual is linked to the actress Sophia Loren, who is quoted as enjoying 'the odd bath in virgin olive oil' as part of her beauty routine.

The appearance goal is softer, more supple-looking skin and a healthy sheen. Olive oil has been used on the body since antiquity, but no clinical trials on olive oil baths themselves were found; claims rest on tradition, celebrity routines and general dermatology about oils as occlusive moisturisers.

paras: Accounts describe a few tablespoons of olive oil poured into a warm bath, a soak of 15-30 minutes, patting the skin dry, and repeating about weekly. Practitioners often pair it with a Mediterranean-style diet, as Loren reportedly did.

Olive oil is heavy and can clog pores or cause breakouts, and the dermatologist quoted by Grazia advises people with oily or acne-prone skin to avoid it. Patch testing is commonly suggested for sensitive skin, and residual oil makes tubs slippery.

lead: Olive oil baths are a skin-care ritual in which virgin olive oil is added to bath water. The actress Sophia Loren is the figure most often linked to it; a beauty article quotes her as enjoying 'the odd bath in virgin olive oil', although the source and date of the quote are not given. Grazia reported that she poured capfuls into baths to keep her skin soft [1].

The idea draws on a long tradition: Greek athletes oiled their bodies in gymnasia from about the 7th century BC and cosmetic olive oil use spread across the Hellenic world [2]. Modern guides present the bath as a way to leave skin hydrated and smooth.
No clinical trials on olive oil baths were located; dermatologists quoted in the lifestyle press describe olive oil as hydrating and barrier-supportive in general, but heavy for some skin types [1].
infobox: Virgin or extra virgin olive oil

paras: The practice adds olive oil to warm bath water. Dermatologist Dara Spearman, quoted by Grazia, described olive oil as providing hydration, antioxidant activity and barrier support, while noting that it is heavy and may clog pores [1].

Spartans and other Greeks rubbed oil on their bodies while exercising, and cosmetic use of olive oil spread through the Hellenic city-states for close to a thousand years [2]. The Loren association is modern celebrity lore and is retold in beauty media [1].

Grazia's version suggests two to four tablespoons in warm bath water, a soak of 15-20 minutes, once weekly or twice for very dry skin, and cleaning the tub afterwards because the residue is slippery [1]. People with oily or acne-prone skin are advised to avoid the approach [1].
